passages.happening:
David and the army commanders set apart sons of Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun ‘to prophesy with the accompaniment of lyres, harps, and cymbals’ (verse 1). Each group serves under its father, and the fathers serve under the king (verses 2-3, 6). Jeduthun ‘prophesied with the harp, giving thanks and praise to the LORD’ (verse 3).

Heman, ‘the king’s seer’ (verse 5), has fourteen sons and three daughters, given to him ‘through the promises of God to exalt him’ (verse 5). With their relatives, all ‘trained and skillful in the songs of the LORD, they numbered 288’ (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
After the Levites and the priests come the musicians. They led the music when the ark came up in chapter 15 and gave thanks before it in chapter 16; now the arrangement is made permanent for the temple. Worship in Solomon's house will be sacrifice and song together. Who to notice: the three leaders, Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun.

They came from the three Levite clans, and their names stand in the book of Psalms. Twelve psalms are headed with Asaph's name, Psalm 50 and Psalms 73 to 83; Psalm 88 names Heman the Ezrahite; and Jeduthun appears in the headings of Psalms 39, 62 and 77. Jeduthun seems to be the Ethan of chapter 15. Scholars discuss whether the headings mean the men themselves or the musical guilds that bore their names, since sons of Asaph could describe a guild as well as a family.

The word prophesy surprises modern readers, who think of prediction. In the Old Testament it has a wider range, including inspired speech and song in worship. Saul once met a band of prophets coming down with harps, tambourines, flutes and lyres, and Elisha asked for a harpist before he prophesied. The songs of thanks and praise were understood as Spirit-given speech about God, and Heman is called a seer, chozeh, the title given to Gad. A large family was counted as honor and wealth in that culture.

The last nine names of Heman's sons in verse 4 have caught many scholars' attention. Read together in Hebrew, they sound like a line of prayer, asking the LORD for grace, calling him God, speaking of help and of hardship and asking for visions. Whether they were real names, titles or the opening words of songs is debated.
passages.later: When the second temple's foundation was laid, ‘the Levites (the sons of Asaph) with cymbals, took their positions to praise the LORD, as David king of Israel had prescribed’ (Ezra 3:10). Elisha once said, ‘But now, bring me a harpist’ (2 Kings 3:15).
passages.asks: The musicians' songs were counted as a kind of prophecy, speech about God given by God. Ask what the songs you sing are saying about God, and whether you believe them. And ask whose skill in your church's worship you have taken for granted.

passages.happening: ‘They cast lots for their duties, young and old alike, teacher as well as pupil’ (verse 8). Then twenty-four lots fall in turn, each to a leader with his sons and brothers, twelve in all, ending with ‘the twenty-fourth to Romamti-ezer, his sons, and his brothers’ (verse 31).
passages.hearers:
The list follows one formula twenty-four times: the number, the name, his sons and his brothers, twelve in all. Twenty-four courses of twelve make the 288 of verse 7, matching the twenty-four courses of priests in chapter 24. The steady repetition mirrors what it describes, a rotation of voices that never stops.

The lot was cast young and old alike, teacher as well as pupil. Neither age nor skill nor rank settled who sang when. In a list where every man is named by his father, that line quietly sets every singer on the same footing before God.

After the exile, singers descended from Asaph came back from Babylon, and they led the praise when the second temple's foundation was laid. For the Chronicler's first readers, these were the ancestors of the singers still serving in their own temple.
passages.later: After the exile the returning families included ‘The singers: the descendants of Asaph, 128’ (Ezra 2:41).
passages.asks: Teacher and pupil drew lots alike. Ask whether you serve more gladly when you lead than when you learn. And ask who has taught you to sing your faith, and whether you have thanked them.
